identify.title: You hired someone so you’d never have to look at this again.

one.statement: Your best seller hit zero on a Tuesday.
one.body: You found out Friday, from a customer.

two.statement: The low-stock alert fired at 10 units.
two.body: For that product, 10 units is two days. For the slow one next to it, 10 units is a month. Same alert. Useless both times.

three.statement: So you ordered big. Just to be safe.
three.body: Now there’s a pallet of it in the 3PL, and the cash you needed for the next thing is sitting on a shelf.

four.statement: Meanwhile the spreadsheet says your best seller is a slow mover.
four.body: Because every day it was sold out counted as a day nobody wanted it.

identify.closer: You’re still the one who notices.

logic.title: Days of cover, against the supplier you actually use

one.title: Your best seller stops looking slow
one.body: Its sell rate is measured on the days it could actually be bought — so the products that move fastest stop being the ones that get under-ordered.

two.title: You hear about it in time to order
two.body: The warning is days of cover against your supplier’s real lead time — not a unit count. Nine days left with a 3-day supplier is fine. Nine days left with a 26-day supplier is already late. Runway knows the difference.

three.title: Every line prices the order
three.body: It says what the order costs and how long the cash is tied up. “282 short. Ordering costs $9,900, tied up about 74 days.” You can say no to that — and be right.

logic.footer: Every number shows its working: check it once against your admin, then stop checking. And your stock history starts the day you install — Shopify keeps only today’s number, and nothing before install can be recovered, by anyone.

objections.title: The four reasons not to believe this — answered

one.q: “Shopify already shows me days out of stock.”
one.a: It shows the count. It doesn’t keep the history, doesn’t fix the sell rate, and doesn’t tell you what the reorder ties up.

two.a: At 10 units, whether that’s two days or twenty. They fire too late to do anything about it — that’s the most common complaint in the category.

three.a: The alert, maybe. Not the history. Shopify doesn’t store it, and you can’t build yesterday. It exists only if something has been recording it.

four.a: There isn’t one to check. One list a week to whoever runs inventory. One line a month to you.

confess.title: We built the lost-revenue number too — then buried it.
confess.sub: Every tool in this category has one, and every one of them is a guess dressed as a fact. Ours is on the line as evidence, never as the headline — and it shows you the floor, the middle, and the guess everyone else prints as truth.

solution.title: You stop being the one who notices.
solution.sub: Best sellers on the shelf. Cash not stuck in the rest.
solution.withoutBody: You find out at zero. You order big to make it stop. The cash gets stuck. And you’re still the one who has to notice.
solution.withBody: Monday, one list. What’s running out, when, how much, what it ties up. Someone acts on it. Once a month, one line to you: what got reordered before it hit zero, and what didn’t.
